page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.t5-c1m1.xlarge is a shared, burstable virtual instance operating on KVM virtualization and the x86_64 architecture. Compute is driven by an Intel Xeon 8163 processor running at a base clock speed of 2.5 GHz. The instance configuration allocates 4 vCPUs derived from 2 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled. Cache configuration includes 32 KB of L1 data cache, 1.0 MB of L2 cache, and a shared 33 MB L3 cache. Instruction set extensions include AVX, AVX-512F, AES, and BMI2. Memory capacity totals 4.0 GB, establishing a 1:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio of 1.0 GB per core. The instance includes no onboard local storage, relying on external network-attached storage, and provides a 1 Gbps baseline network bandwidth profile without bundled public IPv4 addresses.

Benchmark measurements reflect the burstable and resource-constrained nature of the underlying hardware allocation. In single-core compute testing, stress-ng produced 1018.78 and Geekbench yielded 814.0, placing the instance in the bottom ten percent of tested servers. Multi-core performance registered 4021.29 on stress-ng and 2382.0 on Geekbench, both residing within the bottom quartile. Compression and decompression tests returned modest throughput, with gzip compression recording 19.01 GB/sec and multi-threaded bzip3 decompression achieving 10.55 GB/sec. Large block uncached memory write throughput performed moderately at 26.9 GB/sec, while read throughput reached 28.46 GB/sec. Application testing yielded 3.96 million operations per second for Redis SET requests, alongside 2.44 GB/sec for static web serving.

The primary architectural tradeoff of ecs.t5-c1m1.xlarge lies in its low memory-per-core density combined with burstable CPU limits, which restrict sustained high-intensity computation and memory-heavy execution paths. From a cost-efficiency perspective, the shared hardware tier provides economical access to 4 vCPUs for intermittent execution patterns that do not justify dedicated compute resources. The instance fits non-production staging environments, lightweight microservices, scheduled batch scripts, low-volume web endpoints, and testing pipelines where burst capacity is sufficient and continuous CPU saturation is not required.
